activities.criteria: Include money, quantity, identity and referential-integrity rules.

activities.prompt: Deliver schema, seed data, query notebook, application integration and automated regression checks.
activities.criteria: Another learner can recreate the database and check expected results.

activities.prompt: Run a concurrent-stock test and a restore drill; include exact reproduction steps and observations.
activities.criteria: No negative stock or duplicate reservations; restore meets your stated test objectives.

activities.prompt: Defend two index choices, one migration and one recovery decision in a design review.
activities.criteria: Support decisions with measured workload and acknowledge remaining limitations.

coach.before: A complete project combines schema design, correct queries, safe writes, and operational readiness.
coach.worked: Acceptance check for money: SELECT SUM(balance) FROM accounts. If transfers are wrapped in transactions, this total should never change during concurrent transfers between accounts.
steps: Define the system invariant (e.g., total money is constant).
Write a query to measure this invariant.
Run concurrent operations (like transfers).
Compare the before and after totals. A matching total supports this invariant for the tested cases; also inspect per-account balances and failed-transfer behavior.
coach.question: If a transfer fails halfway and is not rolled back, what happens to the sum?
coach.feedback: A partial update means money was created or destroyed, changing the total and proving the system is not transactionally safe.
coach.guided: Write a query to check that no order items reference a missing order. Expect zero rows.
coach.independent: Write an invariant query to ensure stock quantity is never negative. Expect zero rows violating this.
coach.boundary: The browser lab cannot run real concurrent stress tests or verify actual network integrations and end-to-end latency.

levels.title: Start with tables
levels.description: See how a computer stores facts and how to find one small answer.

levels.title: Ask useful questions
levels.description: Select, filter, combine and summarize information.

levels.title: Keep changes correct and quick
levels.description: Learn what happens when several changes or searches occur.

levels.title: Build and protect a database
levels.description: Explore the extra tools that help teams keep data reliable.

levels.title: Make a complete data project
levels.description: Design, query and review a small database from beginning to end.

tracks.title: Salesforce: from a small change to a safe release
tracks.subtitle: Understand how teams review and deliver software changes
tracks.prerequisite: No Salesforce, Git or coding experience needed. First learn what a change is; the practice simulator works without an account.
tracks.promise: Follow a change from an idea to a checked and reviewed release. Advanced lessons explain the real tools and safe setup.

modules.title: Understand a release end to end
modules.concept: Salesforce metadata describes application structure and behavior; business records are data. Git tracks the chosen metadata files. CI validates a proposed change; deployment applies accepted changes to a target org. Start with a disposable learning org and a clearly named target.
modules.example: Changing a field definition is metadata work. Changing one customer record is data work. A validation may test a proposed deployment without applying the change; a passing check is not proof the target was actually updated.
modules.plain: A Salesforce change may update a screen, a rule or a saved record. Teams check changes before sharing them.
modules.analogy: A classroom app has settings and student records; changing the rule is different from editing one student’s record.
terms: One Salesforce workspace used by a team.
The setup and rules that describe how an app works.
One saved item of business information.

activities.prompt: Draw feature branch → pull request → validation → approval → merge → deployment → verification.
activities.criteria: Distinguish review, validation and deployment boundaries.

activities.prompt: Inventory a sample object, field, Apex class and permission set; label dependencies and intended target.
activities.criteria: Keep org identity explicit and use fake business data.

activities.prompt: Explain why a green validation does not prove a field exists in the production org.
activities.criteria: Validation and deployment are different actions against stated targets.

activities.prompt: Write a release acceptance checklist including a post-deployment functional check.
activities.criteria: Verify behavior and permissions after deployment, not only job status.

coach.before: Before deploying, understand the target. Metadata is the configuration and logic. Records are the actual business data entries.
coach.worked: To add a new 'Shoe Size' tracking feature, we deploy the metadata defining the field. We do not deploy specific users' shoe sizes. Validation checks if this field can deploy safely.
steps: Identify the required metadata
Run a validation dry-run
Deploy the metadata
Verify the field exists in the org
coach.question: Does a successful validation dry-run mean the feature is available to users?
choices: No, validation only checks if a deployment would succeed
coach.feedback: Validation does not save changes. A real deployment must follow.
coach.guided: Classify: one request with Subject=Broken keyboard is data; the definition of Subject__c is metadata. Expected classifications: data, metadata.
coach.independent: A new Due_Date__c definition is metadata; a request’s due date 2026-10-12 is data. Verify the field exists and a fictional record accepts a date after actual deployment.
coach.boundary: Browser simulators simulate job statuses, but they cannot verify configuration inside a real Salesforce org.

modules.title: Use Git as an audit trail
modules.concept: A commit records a snapshot with a parent history. Branches name moving points in that history. A pull request proposes a merge and collects checks and review. Small changes make both review and failure diagnosis easier. Conflict resolution must preserve intended behavior, not simply remove conflict markers.
modules.example: Two branches change the same permission set. Git may detect a textual conflict, but a clean merge can still create a semantic conflict such as unintentionally broad access. Review the resulting metadata and test behavior.
modules.plain: Git keeps a history of changes so a team can see what changed and work on ideas safely.
modules.analogy: Save labelled copies of a group assignment so you can see who changed what and return to an earlier version.
terms: A tool that records changes to files.
A labelled save point in the project history.
A separate line of work for trying a change.

activities.prompt: Draw a main branch and two feature branches, then a merge commit.
activities.criteria: Identify parent relationships and compare the correct revisions.

activities.prompt: Create a small local repo; make two independent commits and inspect each diff before committing.
activities.criteria: Commits are focused, messages explain intent, and no credentials are tracked.

activities.prompt: Resolve a deliberate conflict in a disposable branch and document the intended combined result.
activities.criteria: Test the merged behavior rather than only accepting one side.

activities.prompt: Write a pull-request description with problem, behavior, tests and risk for a field change.
activities.criteria: Reviewer can assess the change without private conversational context.

coach.before: Git records changes. A commit is a snapshot. A branch isolates work. Merging combines text, but doesn't prove it works.
coach.worked: Two developers edit the same permission set on different branches. Git merges the text cleanly, but the combined permissions might grant too much access. The logic must be re-tested.
steps: Create two branches
Commit changes independently
Merge branches
Test the combined behavior
coach.question: If Git reports no merge conflicts, what is guaranteed?
choices: The code will compile and pass tests
The text lines were combined without overlap
The metadata is ready for production
coach.feedback: Git only handles text. A clean text merge can still result in broken business logic.
coach.guided: Two branches change one setting: branch A says Read; branch B says Edit. Expected: the reviewer must choose the intended access; taking both blindly is not a security review.
coach.independent: Write a PR for adding Due_Date__c: include purpose, changed files, empty-date and valid-date test results, and permission impact. Expected: a reviewer can reproduce both tests.
coach.boundary: The simulation shows text merges but cannot execute Salesforce syntax checks on the combined code.

modules.title: Structure reproducible metadata work
modules.concept: A reproducible project declares what is tracked and how tools run. Metadata components depend on one another, so deployment units need more than changed filenames. Deletions require explicit handling; removing a file from Git alone does not guarantee removal in an org.
modules.example: A new field used by Apex needs both components and appropriate permissions. A destructive change should target a disposable component, prove dependency impact, and include recovery or reconstruction steps.
modules.plain: A project is easier to share when its files are in familiar places and its instructions can be repeated.
modules.analogy: Keep worksheets, answers and teacher notes in labelled folders instead of one mixed pile.
terms: A project folder with its change history.
A list of the files or parts included in a change.
A set of steps a computer can run automatically.

activities.prompt: Map a sample field, class and permission set to project files and dependencies.
activities.criteria: Explain why the deployment unit may contain more than one changed file.

activities.prompt: Retrieve one harmless metadata component into a disposable project and inspect the diff.
activities.criteria: Record org identity, tool versions and reproducible steps; keep tokens out of output.

activities.prompt: Design a validation case for a missing dependency and explain the error evidence you expect.
activities.criteria: Relate the error to the missing metadata instead of changing unrelated permissions.

activities.prompt: Plan a deletion rehearsal with explicit approval, dependency checks and post-deletion verification.
activities.criteria: Use a throwaway component and a reconstructable definition; do not experiment on production.

coach.before: Source code lives in structured folders. force-app holds Salesforce metadata. .github/workflows holds automation scripts.
coach.worked: Deleting a custom field requires a destructiveChanges.xml file. We must identify any dependencies, like classes using the field, and plan a recovery before deleting.
steps: Identify the metadata to remove
Trace dependencies
Write the destructive manifest
Rehearse the deletion on a throwaway component
coach.question: Why should you practice destructive changes on a disposable component?
choices: Because production environments reject all deletions
To safely learn the process without permanently losing real configuration
coach.feedback: Never experiment on live configuration. Practice with disposable items to understand dependencies.
coach.guided: Illustration: Apex class references Due_Date__c but package contains only the class. Expected missing dependency: the field definition.
coach.independent: For deleting Test_Only__c, list every reference, remove them first in a disposable org and rehearse recovery. Expected: deployment succeeds only after references are resolved; data recovery is separately planned.
coach.boundary: Simulations parse XML paths but cannot calculate the true dependency closure of a real Salesforce environment.

modules.title: Construct a CI workflow
modules.concept: A workflow connects triggers to jobs and steps. A nonzero exit should fail a required check; swallowing it can create a falsely green pipeline. Untrusted pull-request code must not automatically receive privileged credentials. Tool versions and workflow dependencies influence reproducibility.
modules.example: Checkout → install pinned tools → analyze → authenticate when permitted → validate → upload reports. Reports help diagnose failure, but uploading a report must not convert a failed validation into a successful required check.
modules.plain: Automatic checks can look for mistakes every time a team suggests a change.
modules.analogy: A spell-checker reviews a draft before the class turns it in.
terms: Automatic checks that run when code changes.
A practice check that does not yet apply the change.

activities.prompt: Trace which jobs run for a pull request and for a push to the protected branch.
activities.criteria: A pull request validates; accepted changes deploy through a separate authorized path.

activities.prompt: Write a workflow outline with distinct validation and deployment responsibilities.
activities.criteria: Declare events, dependencies, permissions and report artifacts.

activities.prompt: Find a shell step that masks an error with an unconditional success; repair its exit behavior.
activities.criteria: Required failure propagates; diagnostic upload may still run safely.

activities.prompt: Explain handling of forked contributions and why privileged secrets cannot be exposed to arbitrary code.
activities.criteria: Separate trust boundaries; do not use a privileged trigger to execute unchecked contributor code.

coach.before: CI workflows run automatic checks. A validation checks a pull request, while a deployment applies merged code.
coach.worked: A workflow script runs static analysis before validation. If the scanner finds an error, the script must exit with a failure code to block the pipeline from continuing.
steps: Trigger workflow on pull request
Run static analysis script
Propagate any failure exit codes
Proceed to validation only if successful
coach.question: Why must a workflow script propagate failure exit codes?
choices: To stop the pipeline and prevent deploying broken code
To upload the error log to Salesforce
coach.feedback: Suppressing errors creates a false green build. The pipeline must fail to block bad code.
coach.guided: Illustration: scanner exits 1 but a script returns 0 unconditionally. Expected fix: preserve the failing exit code and stop before validation.
coach.independent: Make a two-job plan: PR checks never deploy; main deployment uses the reviewed revision. Expected: failed PR checks block release; successful deployment is verified in the intended org.
coach.boundary: The browser illustrates workflow gates; it does not run a hosted CI workflow or authenticate to Salesforce. Run the actual checks locally or on a free runner, and inspect their exit status.

modules.title: Authenticate with least privilege
modules.concept: Machine authentication establishes an identity; authorization determines its allowed actions. JWT signing uses a private key that must never enter a repository or logs. The connected application configuration, certificate, user approval and target URL must agree. The exact platform setup is version-sensitive, so verify current official instructions before connecting a live org.
modules.example: A valid signature can still fail because the user is not authorized or the audience targets the wrong login service. Giving the integration user administrator access may conceal the actual configuration issue while expanding risk.
modules.plain: A tool must prove who it is before Salesforce allows it to make a change.
modules.analogy: A school badge identifies a person, but a teacher still decides which rooms that person may enter.
terms: Checking who or what is asking.
Checking what that identity is allowed to do.
Information used to check a digital identity.

activities.prompt: Draw the trust flow from runner to signing key, application configuration and target org.
activities.criteria: Identify private versus public material and where each belongs.

activities.prompt: Write an authentication checklist with placeholders only and a minimal integration-user permission plan.
activities.criteria: No real key or token appears in files; permissions correspond to required operations.

activities.prompt: Diagnose three cases: expired certificate, wrong target and unauthorized integration user.
activities.criteria: Use the specific error and identity/target evidence rather than blanket permission escalation.

activities.prompt: Plan certificate rotation with overlap, validation and revocation of the old key.
activities.criteria: A failed rotation has a recovery path; old material is retired after verification.

coach.before: Authentication proves identity. Authorization grants permissions. Both are required for an automated tool to act.
coach.worked: A CI runner signs a JWT with a private key. Salesforce verifies it using a public certificate. The integration user must also be specifically authorized for the connected app and granted minimal permissions.
steps: Provide the private key to the runner
Configure the public certificate in Salesforce
Assign minimal deployment permissions
Authorize the integration user
coach.question: If an integration user has a valid certificate but lacks app authorization, what happens?
choices: The login fails due to lack of authorization
coach.feedback: A valid key is insufficient if the identity is not explicitly authorized for the application.
coach.guided: Place private key only in the runner’s secret storage; public certificate in the Salesforce application. Expected: no private key in Git, screenshots or logs.
coach.independent: On paper, plan a certificate rotation: add the replacement public certificate, update the runner secret, verify login to a practice org, then revoke the old credential. Expected: new login succeeds and old credential is denied. Continuity depends on the application’s supported rotation process.
coach.boundary: Simulators handle fake tokens. Real authentication requires managing active secrets securely in a vault.

modules.title: Protect credentials and enforce reviews
modules.concept: A policy written in a file is different from a policy enforced by repository or environment settings. CODEOWNERS identifies reviewers; required review enforcement depends on configured rules and plan capabilities. Scope credentials narrowly and avoid printing them while debugging. Treat accidental exposure as a revocation problem, not only a file-removal problem.
modules.example: Deleting a committed key from the latest file does not remove it from prior Git history. Rotate or revoke the credential first, then coordinate history cleanup and investigate usage. A secret-shaped test string can safely demonstrate scanner behavior.
modules.plain: Keep passwords and private keys out of shared files, and require a real review before important changes.
modules.analogy: A key stays with the person who needs it; it is not taped to the front door.
terms: Private information that can unlock an account or system.
A person checking a proposed change before it is accepted.
A file that suggests who should review certain changes.

activities.prompt: Create a matrix of which workflow and environment may read each placeholder secret.
activities.criteria: Least privilege is explicit for both identities and execution contexts.

activities.prompt: Define review and required-check rules, including stale approval after new commits.
activities.criteria: Distinguish file declarations from platform-enforced rules.

activities.prompt: Rehearse a leaked-placeholder incident: detection, revocation plan, investigation and cleanup.
activities.criteria: No real credentials are used; removal from the newest commit alone is insufficient.

activities.prompt: Explain how to verify protections actually prevent an unauthorized merge in your chosen hosting plan.
activities.criteria: Record an attempted blocked action and observed behavior; do not assume unavailable paid features exist.

coach.before: Secrets must never be committed to source code. Review rules protect against unauthorized changes.
coach.worked: A deleted secret can remain in Git history and copies. Immediately revoke or rotate it at the provider; then remove exposure according to the incident plan. History cleanup alone cannot invalidate a copied credential.
steps: Identify the leaked credential
Immediately revoke it at the provider
Clean the repository history
Implement secure placeholders
coach.question: Why does deleting a leaked key in the next commit fail to protect the system?
choices: It takes too long to process
Git retains the full history of previous commits, leaving the key exposed
coach.feedback: Git tracks history. Anyone can check out the previous commit and read the leaked secret.
coach.guided: Replace a fake inline token with a secret reference. Expected: no token value in the staged diff. Never practice with a real token.
coach.independent: Fake token found in an old commit: record revoke/rotate, verify old token is denied, audit use, clean exposure and update dependent apps. Expected: deletion alone is rejected as a complete fix.
coach.boundary: Browser labs use dummy strings. Real credential leakage requires coordinating revocation with your cloud provider.

modules.title: Compute and validate a safe delta
modules.concept: A delta represents differences between two selected revisions. The correct base depends on the release process and last successful deployment, not simply the previous commit. Missing history or the wrong comparison can omit necessary changes. Empty deltas and destructive changes need explicit handling.
modules.example: If deployment of commit B failed and C later succeeds, comparing only B→C may omit changes introduced at B. Comparing the last successfully deployed baseline A→C captures the intended cumulative change.
modules.plain: A safe release contains the changes you meant to make, including removals, and nothing unexpected.
modules.analogy: Compare a packing list with what is already in the suitcase before deciding what to add or remove.
terms: The difference between an earlier and a later version.
The last known version used for comparison.
A saved package produced by a build or check.

activities.prompt: Draw A→B→C with failed deployment B; identify the correct release baseline.
activities.criteria: Use last successful target baseline A when that is the process contract.

activities.prompt: Create a disposable Git example with additions, modifications and deletions; inspect the generated change set.
activities.criteria: Account for deletions and dependencies, not just added files.

activities.prompt: Diagnose an empty or incomplete delta caused by shallow history or a wrong base.
activities.criteria: Verify fetched revisions and comparison semantics before rerunning deployment.

activities.prompt: Design an immutable deployment artifact that records source revision, baseline, manifest and validation result.
activities.criteria: The approved artifact and deployed artifact can be tied to the same source revision.

coach.before: A delta contains only the differences between two points. Setting the correct baseline is critical.
coach.worked: Baseline A was deployed successfully. Commit B adds Priority__c but its deployment fails. C also adds a Flow referencing Priority__c. Compare A to C: the package needs the field AND Flow plus their dependencies. Comparing B to C omits the never-deployed field.
steps: Find the last successful deployment baseline
Identify the head commit
Calculate the delta
Verify the resulting package includes all expected changes
coach.question: What happens if a delta is calculated using a shallow git clone without history?
choices: The delta may be empty or missing necessary files
coach.feedback: Delta tools require the actual commit history to compare files properly.
coach.guided: Release log: A success, B failure, C proposed. Expected baseline: A, not B.
coach.independent: A has neither field nor Flow; B adds field but fails; C adds Flow using that field. Expected package: field + Flow and required dependencies, plus a reviewed deletion plan if applicable.
coach.boundary: Simulated deltas compare text files. Real Salesforce deltas must respect metadata API boundaries and folder structures.

modules.title: Make quality gates meaningful
modules.concept: Tests need assertions about behavior, not merely executed lines. Static analysis finds certain classes of issues without running the program; it complements tests. Test level and coverage requirements depend on deployment context. Preserve test reports and classify failures before retrying.
modules.example: A test that creates a record but asserts nothing can execute code while missing a regression. A useful test states expected behavior and includes bulk and negative cases where relevant to Apex limits and contracts.
modules.plain: Tests are examples that check whether a change behaves the way the team expects.
modules.analogy: Try a light switch several times before trusting that it works every time.
terms: A repeatable check of expected behavior.
A statement that a result must match an expectation.
A count of which lines ran during tests; it does not prove they were correct.

activities.prompt: Compare line coverage with a behavioral assertion and describe what each proves.
activities.criteria: High coverage alone does not demonstrate correctness.

activities.prompt: Write a test plan for an Apex change including bulk inputs, permissions and expected failures.
activities.criteria: Each scenario has an expected outcome and reproducible setup.

activities.prompt: Classify a failed run into syntax, analyzer finding, assertion failure, limits or target configuration.
activities.criteria: Choose the next investigation step using the report evidence.

activities.prompt: Define a gate policy including report retention and justified handling of flaky tests.
activities.criteria: Do not silently ignore failures or rerun indefinitely until green.

coach.before: Tests are assertions of expected behavior. Code coverage only proves lines executed, not that they are correct.
coach.worked: An Apex test runs business logic and explicitly asserts that the final result matches the expectation. A useful test must include negative inputs and check bulk processing limits.
steps: Prepare test records
Execute the target business logic
Assert the actual result against the expected outcome
Verify behavior under bulk limits
coach.question: Does high line coverage guarantee that code behaves correctly?
choices: No, lines can execute without asserting the correct business outcome
Yes, if it runs in production
coach.feedback: Coverage tracks execution. Only meaningful assertions verify correctness.
coach.guided: For a 10% discount on 100, assert actual price equals 90, not merely that the calculation ran.
coach.independent: Design tests for 0 open requests→0, one New + one Closed with notes→1, and 200 New→200. Add a restricted-user check; count assertions alone do not prove permission safety.
coach.boundary: Simulations execute basic logic checks. Real Apex limits, bulk behaviors, and database transactions only occur on Salesforce servers.

modules.title: Release, observe and recover
modules.concept: A release must target the intended environment and the reviewed revision. Prevent overlapping deployments from racing when the process cannot safely handle them. Record what was deployed and verify behavior afterward. Rollback is not automatically a complete reversal: schema, dependencies and data changes may require forward repair.
modules.example: A deployment succeeds but users cannot access a new field. The release check needs permissions and a user-level smoke test. Re-deploying older metadata may not reconstruct deleted business data.
modules.plain: A release is a checked change sent to the right place, followed by a check that it worked.
modules.analogy: A rehearsal and a real performance are separate events; after the show, check that the audience can see and hear.
terms: Applying a change to a chosen Salesforce workspace.
A separate place for building, testing or using software.
Returning to an earlier state when that is safe and possible.

activities.prompt: Create a release timeline from accepted revision to target verification with responsibility at each step.
activities.criteria: Keep revision, target, approval and job identifiers together.

activities.prompt: Write a runbook for deploying one harmless field to a disposable org and checking access as a representative user.
activities.criteria: Verify actual behavior and permission expectations beyond the job status.

activities.prompt: Simulate a post-release permission failure and choose rollback versus forward repair with reasoning.
activities.criteria: State what can and cannot be reversed; protect data separately.

activities.prompt: Design concurrency control and a deployment ledger so the next release knows the target baseline.
activities.criteria: A failed or canceled run never advances the successful baseline.

coach.before: A deployment changes the target environment. Observation confirms the change. A rollback reverses metadata.
coach.worked: After deploying a new field, we verify users can actually access it. If a deployment fails or causes issues, we can roll back the metadata, but we cannot easily restore deleted business data.
steps: Execute the deployment
Perform a post-release verification
Observe user permissions
Decide to rollback or fix forward
coach.question: Why is rolling back a deployment not a universal fix?
choices: Rolling back metadata might not recover deleted business data records
coach.feedback: Metadata changes can be reverted, but data lost or altered by those changes often requires manual restoration.
coach.guided: After adding Due_Date__c, check a permitted staff user can enter a date and an unpermitted user cannot edit it. Expected: both access checks match the matrix.
coach.independent: Rehearse reverting a disposable field definition. Expected: old metadata can be restored when dependencies allow; deleted field values are not assumed recovered by a Git revert.
coach.boundary: A browser lab simulates job states. Real deployments require verifying actual user visibility and integration logs.

modules.title: Operate a multi-environment delivery system
modules.concept: Promote an identified change through environments with explicit gates. Environment-specific credentials and configuration must not be copied blindly. Drift happens when org changes escape the declared source process. Operate the pipeline with evidence: cycle time, failure categories, recovery time and a record of decisions.
modules.example: Build once and promote an identified artifact where the toolchain permits, with target-specific configuration applied deliberately. If an administrator changes metadata directly, detect and reconcile the drift before the next release overwrites it.
modules.plain: A team may move a change through several workspaces, with a check and an approval at each important step.
modules.analogy: A school play goes from practice to a dress rehearsal, then to the performance, with checks along the way.
terms: Moving an approved change to the next workspace.
A difference that appeared outside the team’s planned changes.
A problem that needs a clear response and record.

activities.prompt: Draw a dev→test→UAT→production path with distinct identities and approvals.
activities.criteria: Each transition has a condition and an accountable decision.

activities.prompt: Deliver a demonstration repository, workflow, test report, deployment ledger and operator guide using a disposable org.
activities.criteria: A second learner can reproduce the demo; no credentials are included.

activities.prompt: Run three incident drills: authentication failure, failed Apex test and incorrect delta baseline.
activities.criteria: For each drill capture symptom, first useful evidence, repair and prevention.

activities.prompt: Present a release review explaining traceability, least privilege, recovery limits and the next improvement.
activities.criteria: Support claims with artifacts and identify features dependent on the chosen hosting plan.

coach.before: A mature system promotes artifacts through isolated environments. Unplanned changes cause drift.
coach.worked: We build a package once and promote it to Dev, UAT, and Production. If an admin edits Production directly, they create drift. We must pull that drift into source control before the next release overwrites it.
steps: Build an immutable artifact
Promote the artifact to UAT
Test and approve
Promote the exact same artifact to Production
coach.question: What is the danger of manual drift in a production environment?
choices: It makes the system run faster
The next automated release may overwrite the manual changes
coach.feedback: Automated pipelines deploy what is in source control. Manual changes not in source will be overwritten.
coach.guided: Repository says Priority=Low/Medium/High; practice org also has Critical. Expected drift: Critical exists only in org; reconcile and review before deploying.
coach.independent: Record one immutable revision, local test output, practice-org rehearsal, reviewer decision and post-deploy check. Expected: deployed revision matches the reviewed one; a documented previous revision can be redeployed where metadata dependencies permit.
coach.boundary: The browser illustrates release decisions. Rehearse on two free practice orgs with fictional data and locally run checks; real company production/sandbox access and CI features depend on its own plan. No paid environments are required for this course.
